title: Sudan As A Mirror For Today’s World | NOEMA
gist: Young and Ali argue Sudan's war is not anarchy but a reversion to pre-colonial and 19th-century patterns of trade routes, merchant-warlord states and autonomous borderlands, as colonial-era infrastructure and the liberal order that sustained it decay. The RSF's gold-and-desert-route model echoes Zubayr Pasha's merchant empire.

insights.claim: Sudan has repeatedly served as a laboratory for multilateral intervention, from the troika-mediated end of the 1983-2005 civil war to two large UN/AU peacekeeping missions, so today's Western disengagement there is a telling signal of the liberal world order's decline.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Treat Western retreat from conflict mediation as a structural regime change that raises tail risk across fragile states.
insights.locator: Sudan has often served as a mirror

insights.claim: The UN General Assembly's 2005 adoption of Responsibility to Protect, rooted in Francis Deng's idea of 'sovereignty as responsibility' developed amid Sudan's wars, marked the high-water point of liberal world order legitimacy.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Provides a benchmark date for how far norm-based intervention has receded since.
insights.locator: It was in this context

insights.claim: Since April 2023 at least 14 million Sudanese have been internally displaced and at least 4.4 million have fled as refugees, burdening Chad, Egypt and South Sudan, with fighting persisting in Kordofan, Darfur and Blue Nile.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Spillover pressure on neighbouring states with weak fiscal capacity is a regional instability channel to monitor.
insights.locator: Today, the conflict in Sudan can be described as a world war in microcosm

insights.claim: Sudan has become a plaything for outside actors from the Middle East and Africa to Russia, Ukraine and Colombia, while US cuts to USAID have reduced even the commitment to prevent famine.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Aid retrenchment plus proxy involvement raises odds of prolonged conflict and famine in the Horn region.
insights.locator: In many ways, what is happening in Sudan

insights.claim: The authors reject the view that Sudan's breakdown is anarchy, arguing instead that it is a return to pre-colonial political and trade patterns, contra Anne Applebaum's claim that the liberal order has ended with nothing to replace it.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Forecast fragmentation using historical state-formation models rather than assuming unstructured chaos.
insights.quote: what is taking place in Sudan and elsewhere is not the emergence of anarchy; it is a return to precolonial patterns
insights.locator: But what is taking place in Sudan

insights.claim: Colonial states endured not because they smashed African societies but because of the durability of the infrastructure they built, so as the liberal order that maintained that infrastructure decays, the colonial-era order dissolves.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Infrastructure chokepoints are the real source of state revenue and control; their decay predicts state weakening.
insights.quote: what looks like chaos is simply the dissolution of the political orders that made colonial and postcolonial state investments durable
insights.locator: But what if what looks like chaos

insights.claim: Timothy Mitchell argues that around 1900 a political technology for discounting the future was invented, and that large transport, energy and irrigation schemes depended on durable arrangements of law, authority and compulsion as well as material durability.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Long-lived infrastructure value rests on institutions; when they erode, asset durability and financing assumptions fail.
insights.locator: In his new book, The Alibi of Capital

insights.claim: Sudan's Gezira irrigation scheme, planned in the 1920s to irrigate over a million acres as a cotton farm for the British Empire, shaped the country's railways, dams, ports, labour force and finance until its financial problems in the 1970s, and oil-era pipelines and refineries later followed colonial-era siting.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Path dependence of infrastructure explains why commodity export control stayed centralised for decades.
insights.locator: Sudan, though often imagined as a colonial backwater

insights.claim: Sudan's export base moved from cotton to crude oil to gold, and unlike cotton or oil, artisanal gold lacks central infrastructural chokepoints the state can tax, so the state cannot capture the trade.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Gold flows from conflict zones are structurally untaxable by central governments, enabling armed non-state financing.
insights.locator: While cotton and crude petroleum are different commodities

insights.claim: Gold prices have risen almost 200% since Sudan's gold export boom began in 2013, and the Sudanese state lost this windfall through incapacity and then war.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Rising gold prices amplify the value of uncontrolled mining revenue to warring factions.
insights.locator: The boom in gold exports from Sudan since 2013

insights.claim: Gold from Darfur mines often reaches Dubai souks without passing through Sudan's central government, reflecting a regional collapse of the taboo against dealing with subnational actors.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Gulf trading hubs are channels for conflict gold; watch provenance and sanctions exposure.
insights.locator: The other dilemma for the Sudanese state

insights.claim: The RSF operates as a paramilitary-slash-merchant company, managing large parts of Sudan on behalf of investors, and its soldiers guarding the Saudi-Yemeni border can be hired out without contracting with the SAF.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Private military-commercial models are an emerging form of state capacity substitute.
insights.locator: The RSF, a paramilitary-slash-merchant company

insights.claim: During the first two years of the war the RSF held Khartoum and tried to break the colonial-era trade route running from provinces through Khartoum to Port Sudan, while the government retreated to Port Sudan and the RSF set up a rival capital in Nyala.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Red Sea port control and the old customs corridor are the state's revenue core; its disruption weakens the government fiscally.
insights.locator: During the first few decades following Sudan's independence

insights.claim: The RSF has revived desert trade routes such as the Darb El Arba'in to Asyut in Egypt, routes north into Libya where it is suspected of bases under Khalifa Haftar's protection, and routes from southern Darfur through South Sudan toward Uganda, Kenya and the Central African Republic, all outside central control.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Supply lines through Libya and East Africa mean regional actors have stakes; trade and smuggling corridors should be monitored.
insights.locator: But perhaps more dramatically, the war saw the re-emergence of old trade routes

insights.claim: In April 2025, two years after the war began, the TASIS Sudan Founding Alliance declared a rival government from Nairobi, uniting the RSF, part of SPLM-N and the Baggara confederation of over six million people stretching from southern Kordofan to Lake Chad.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: A parallel government with cross-border constituencies raises the likelihood of de facto partition.
insights.locator: The new prominence of the old trade routes

insights.claim: The RSF's capture of El Fasher at the end of October 2025 took the last major Darfur stronghold and solidified its resupply routes north through Libya and south across South Sudan into East Africa.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: RSF consolidation of Darfur makes a negotiated reunification less likely.
insights.locator: Initially, Zubayr's base was in the southern borderlands

insights.claim: The RSF's structure, built around Muhammad Hamdan Daglo's Darfurian Arab family and founded in 2013, echoes Zubayr Pasha's 1860s-70s private merchant empire in Bahr al-Ghazal and Darfur, which fielded about 12,000 soldiers, many enslaved, and conquered the Fur Sultanate at El Fasher in 1874.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Merchant-warlord states that combine trade finance and armies are a recurring template; expect RSF-style actors to endure.
insights.locator: The RSF's organization, founded in 2013

insights.claim: Kordofan's contested status today, with El-Obeid (population over 600,000) under frequent attack, resembles the 19th century when Muhammad Ali's armies partially pacified but could not stably control the region.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Kordofan is the likeliest next major front; watch El-Obeid.
insights.locator: Yet another echo of the 19th century

insights.claim: SPLM-N factions straddle the war, with Al-Hilu in the Nuba Mountains siding with the RSF and Agar in Blue Nile siding with the SAF, preserving border-region autonomy in a pattern like the Kingdom of Taqali, which pledged vassalage to both Darfur and Sennar to stay autonomous between about 1780 and 1884.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Borderland actors hedge both sides; treat them as autonomy-maximisers when forecasting alliances.
insights.locator: In the process, the two groups have maintained the autonomy

insights.claim: Trans-Saharan, East and Central African, and Sahel-Red Sea trade routes are re-emerging as the infrastructure and institutions of the liberal order decay, replacing patterns once seen as inevitable parts of the postcolonial world.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Reassess logistics and risk assumptions for the Sahel and Red Sea corridors as trade routes shift away from state-controlled ports.
insights.locator: The breakdown of the Sudanese state we are witnessing today is also not random

insights.claim: Other signs of eroding postwar stability include calls in South Africa to dissolve the Union of South Africa, Yemen's decade-long re-division, and Russian aggression questioning eastern European borders; the 19th-century map is a better model for post-liberal-order statecraft.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Price in more border contestation and shifting boundaries as a baseline geopolitical regime.
insights.quote: it increasingly makes sense to look at the 19th-century map as an example of political competition and shifting boundaries
insights.locator: These are just a few examples
